extracted.intended_audience: individual inventors, lay (pro se) applicants, and small-business owners preparing and prosecuting U.S. patent applications
extracted.subtask_short: drafting and filing U.S. patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, step-by-step guidance for inventors to document, draft, file, prosecute, and maintain U.S. patent applications (including provisional filings, claim drafting, responses to office actions, foreign filing, and commercialization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Full, clear, and accurate written description (full disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the patent application contains a full, clear, and accurate description of how to make and use the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly emphasized as a primary factor in patent quality; the specification must comply with the full disclosure rules. Drafting the specification includes preparing sketches, naming parts, reviewing the specification and abstract carefully, and using checklists provided. Use of AI in drafting is discussed with cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims breadth and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the reach of the patent (technically covered in the patent 'claims') is as broad as possible, given the state of prior developments in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One claim should be as broad as possible. Guidance covers drafting the main (independent) claim, drafting dependent claims, additional sets of claims, the effect of prior art on claims, technical requirements of claims, sample claims, common misconceptions regarding claims, and a checklist for drafting claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability of application to 'sell' the invention's advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the application 'sells' the advantages of the invention (i.e., presents benefits and persuasive description in the application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a core component of patent quality — the application should persuade readers/examiners of the invention's advantages; guidance and checklists throughout the book help structure persuasive elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of applicant's prosecution of correspondence with the PTO
rubrics_metrics.description: How an applicant handles correspondence with the patent office (responses to office actions, amendments, petitions, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes what to do when you receive an Office Action, format for amending specification and claims, drafting the remarks, typing and filing the amendment, consequences if first amendment doesn't result in allowance, petitions (e.g., petition to make special), and Request for Continued Examination (RCE).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal requirements for a utility patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A utility patent must meet four legal requirements: (1) subject matter eligibility, (2) utility, (3) novelty, (4) nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as the core legal eligibility standards for a utility patent; accompanied by a 'Patentability Flowchart' and the admonition 'Don’t make assumptions about the law.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirement #1 for a utility patent: subject matter eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussed in Chapter 5 as a discrete legal requirement for patentability (ties into software/business-method issues and evolving case law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirement #2 for a utility patent: the invention must have utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included among the legal requirements for patentability; evaluate whether the invention is operable and provides a practical purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (35 U.S.C. §102)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirement #3 for a utility patent: the invention must be novel (not anticipated by prior art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treated together with patentability searching and analysis of prior art; influences claim breadth and drafting strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonobviousness (35 U.S.C. §103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirement #4 for a utility patent: the invention must be nonobvious in view of prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how prior art affects claims and patentability; included in the patentability flowchart and search-analysis chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation of invention and conception-recording
rubrics_metrics.description: Documentation is vital: record conception and the building and testing of your invention; how to record your invention and use an invention disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes trade-secret considerations, 'Don’t bury your invention', instructions on how to record, use of invention-disclosure forms, and warning 'Don’t use a "Post Office Patent" to document your invention.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional Patent Application (PPA) use and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the provisional patent application as a substitute for building and testing, with some disadvantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains when to file a PPA, benefits (patent-pending status), and disadvantages compared to a full application; guidance appears in the Documentation and PPA chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability search: whether, how, and quality considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Why to make a patentability search, when not to search, the two ways to make a search, and the fact that the quality of a patent search can vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides inventors on how to hire a patent professional, how to prepare your searcher, how to analyze the search report, DIY computer searching, classification searching, and practical tips for using USPTO tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial viability / marketability evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate your invention for salability: take time to do a commercial feasibility evaluation and check marketability conclusions using consultation and research; build and test if possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 4 provides methods to evaluate commercial potential, start small and ramp up, and techniques for researching markets and consulting potential customers or manufacturers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary work before preparing patent application
rubrics_metrics.description: Do preliminary work—sketches, naming parts, and flowcharts—before preparing the patent application and drafting the specification and drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes checklists for application draft and a sample specification; emphasizes preparing sketches and naming parts first to ease drafting and claim preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification drafting checklist and review
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist for drafting the specification and instructions to review specification and abstract carefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provided as a concrete list in Chapter 8; includes sample patent-application specification and guidance for both paper and EFS-Web finaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting techniques and checklists
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques for drafting independent and dependent claims, additional sets of claims, and use of claim-drafting checklists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers drafting the main independent claim, dependent claims, handling prior art, technical claim requirements, example claims, and a 'Checklist for Drafting Claims.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent drawings: quality, format, and amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: Get your drawings done right; procedures for drawing amendments and submission of corrected drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses how to prepare drawings, Drawing Reference Numerals Worksheet, Submission of Corrected Drawings, and rules for drawing amendments during prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing procedures and timeliness (IDS, EFS-Web, transmittals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Finaling and filing your application (paper vs EFS-Web), filing an Information Disclosure Statement within three months, utility patent transmittals, fee transmittal, and related forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains finaling the specification for paper or EFS-Web filing, the requirement to file the IDS within three months, lists transmittal forms, and includes Appendix 7 downloadable forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to Office Actions and amendment practice
rubrics_metrics.description: What to do when you receive an Office Action, format for amending the specification and claims, drafting the remarks, typing and filing the amendment, and strategies if the first amendment doesn't result in allowance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes a sample Office Action, step-by-step response guidance, and examples of drafting remarks and amendments; covers appeals and pre-appeal brief request procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application continuations, divisionals, CIPs, reissues, and RCEs
rubrics_metrics.description: Options and rules for continuation applications, Requests for Continued Examination (RCE), divisional applications, continuation-in-part (CIP), reissue applications, substitute applications, and double-patenting/terminal disclaimers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 14 explains available supplemental cases and the strategic use of these filings, with summaries of procedure and when to use each branch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-issuance actions: maintenance, enforcement, and commercialization
rubrics_metrics.description: After issue: maintenance fees, patent number marking, checking patents for errors, advertising or selling patents, what rights the patent gives you, legal options for infringement, and commercialization/tax implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 15 covers injunctions, jury trials, arbitration, appeals, patent-forfeiture risks, maintenance fee schedules, enforcement strategies, product clearance, tax deductions, and patent litigation financing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership, assignment, and licensing of inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Who can apply for a patent, inventor/applicant/owner distinctions, joint owners’ agreements, assignment of invention and patent rights, recording assignments with the PTO, and licensing considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 16 gives an overview of licensing (including a Universal License Agreement), recordation procedures, special issues for employed inventors, and how much to seek in licensing deals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign filing strategy and rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on filing abroad: don't file abroad unless the invention has very good prospects in that country; Paris Convention one-year foreign-filing rule; PCT, EPO, Hague Agreement; rescind any nonpublication request and early foreign-filing license/mandatory six-month delay issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 12 explains basics of foreign filing, differences in other countries' patent laws, ways to file abroad, resources, and strategic warnings (e.g., only file abroad when justified).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deciding whether to use an attorney
rubrics_metrics.description: Considerations on whether to do it yourself or hire a patent attorney—factors include cost, time, ability to produce a detailed description and drawings, and personal diligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains pros and cons: the law does not require an attorney; pro se applicants can succeed and PTO offers pro se assistance, but hiring may make sense if you lack time, writing ability, or resources. Also recommends hybrid approaches (do some work yourself, consult an attorney for snags or review).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of checklists and downloadable forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Use checklists and the provided downloadable forms to prepare applications and procedural filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendix 7 lists dozens of downloadable forms (Invention Disclosure, PPA cover sheet, Application Data Sheet, Declarations, IDS forms, petitions, transmittals, RCE transmittal, maintenance fee reminder, assignments, license agreements, etc.). The book repeatedly recommends checklists throughout chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and deadline management
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of time limits (e.g., one-year foreign filing rule, IDS three-month window, maintenance fee deadlines) and procedures for missing or extending PTO deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes a Quick-Reference Timing Chart (Appendix 6), discussion of what to do if you miss or want to extend a PTO deadline, petitions and extensions, and the consequences of missed deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to hire and prepare outside professionals (searchers, drafters, consultants)
rubrics_metrics.description: How to hire a patent professional (searcher or drafter), prepare them for the task, and evaluate the quality of their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapters on searching explain how to hire a patent professional, how to prepare your searcher, and how to analyze a search report; Appendix includes sample consultant and searcher worksheets and agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding common novice-inventor pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: Warnings and anti-patterns such as 'PGL Syndrome', burying your invention, using post office patents to document invention, or failing to build/test when advisable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 2 and Documentation chapters describe common creativity and procedural pitfalls and how to avoid them (e.g., don't sit on your invention; don't rely on ineffective self-documentation methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and limits of AI in patent drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of USPTO guidance and the use of artificial intelligence to draft the specification and claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 22nd edition covers USPTO guidance on using AI in patent applications and includes specific sections 'Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) To Draft the Specification' and 'Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) To Draft Claims'—presumably discussing benefits and caveats.
